one_paragraph_summary: Secretary Roque proposed joint exploration agreements with Chinese companies in the West Philippine Sea -- citing La Bugal-B'laan v. Ramos (December 1, 2004) as support. ACJ Carpio countered that La Bugal covers only land-based minerals, not water-based, and that any arrangement with Chinese companies over areas like Recto Bank would be unconstitutional unless the companies recognize Philippine sovereignty. Panganiban -- as the La Bugal ponente himself -- clarifies: the 246-page, 10-4-1 decision confirms that all natural resources are owned by the state and that their exploration, development, and utilization may be undertaken directly or through coproduction, joint venture, or production-sharing with at least 60%-Filipino corporations; for large-scale mineral or petroleum EDU, the President may also enter financial and technical assistance agreements (FTAAs) with 100%-foreign companies -- provided the Philippines retains 'full control' (like a board of directors retaining residual control) and the President notifies Congress within 30 days. La Bugal nowhere limits its ruling to terrestrial minerals, nor does it authorize 'joint exploration agreements' specifically. But if Roque's proposed arrangements are truly FTAAs -- signed by the President, with full state control, and congressional notification -- then they would be covered by La Bugal, and Carpio's and Roque's positions are not irreconcilable. The column's second section announces 21 FLP and TYKF law scholarships of P200,000 each (10 third-year, 11 fourth-year scholars from Ateneo, UST, UP, FEU, San Beda, and other schools) to be awarded on March 23 at Ateneo Rockwell, with ACJ Carpio as guest of honor and speaker and a board of judges composed of Carpio, de Jesus, Candelaria, Alba, and Gregorio.
